results.title: Jordan's totient at zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$, the Jordan totient function satisfies $J_k(0) = 0$; this is the convention extending $J_k$ to $0$.

results.title: Jordan's totient at one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$, the Jordan totient function satisfies $J_k(1) = 1$.

results.title: Jordan's totient at prime powers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$, every prime $p$ and every integer $e \ge 1$, the Jordan totient function satisfies $J_k(p^e) = p^{k(e-1)}(p^k - 1)$.

results.title: Jordan's totient at primes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$ and every prime $p$, the Jordan totient function satisfies $J_k(p) = p^k - 1$.

results.title: Jordan's totient function is multiplicative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$, the Jordan totient function $J_k$ is multiplicative: $J_k(1) = 1$, and $J_k(mn) = J_k(m) J_k(n)$ for all coprime natural numbers $m$ and $n$.

results.title: Jordan's totient of order one is Euler's totient

results.title: Erdős Problem 822 is true

results.title: Topological 3-manifold
results.caption: Class
results.summary: Let $M$ be a topological space equipped with an atlas of charts, each a homeomorphism from an open subset of $M$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$, whose domains cover $M$. Then $M$ is a topological 3-manifold if it is Hausdorff and second-countable.

results.title: Topological 3-manifold with boundary
results.caption: Class
results.summary: A topological 3-manifold with boundary: a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space locally homeomorphic to the Euclidean half-space `EuclideanHalfSpace 2`.

results.title: Characterization of topological 3-manifolds
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a topological space equipped with an atlas of charts modelled on $\mathbb{R}^3$, so that $M$ is locally homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^3$. Then $M$ is a topological 3-manifold if and only if $M$ is Hausdorff and second-countable.

results.title: Topological 3-manifolds are locally compact
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every topological 3-manifold $M$ is locally compact, since $\mathbb{R}^3$ is.

results.title: Resolvent norm bound for a normal operator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The resolvent norm bound for a normal operator: if `z` lies outside the spectrum of a normal `A`, then `‖(z • 1 - A)⁻¹‖ ≤ 1 / dist z (spectrum ℂ A)`.

results.title: Bauer–Fike theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Bauer–Fike theorem: every point of the spectrum of `A + E` lies within `‖E‖` of the spectrum of a normal operator `A`.

results.title: Attained form of the Bauer–Fike theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The attained form of Bauer–Fike: some eigenvalue-like point of the spectrum of `A` is within `‖E‖` of `μ`.

results.title: Hausdorff distance between spectra of self-adjoint perturbations
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For self-adjoint `A` and `A + E`, the Hausdorff distance of the two spectra is at most `‖E‖`.

results.title: Measurability of the Pólya urn predictive law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The predictive law depends measurably on the previous draws.

results.title: Blackwell–MacQueen urn
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Blackwell–MacQueen urn with parameter `α` and base measure `H`: the joint law of the first `n` draws, where draw `n` has law `polyaUrnPredictive α H xs` given the previous draws `xs` (Blackwell–MacQueen 1973).

results.title: Blackwell–MacQueen urn law is a probability measure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The urn law is a probability measure.

results.title: The predictive rule of the urn
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `P(X₀ ∈ A₀, …, X_n ∈ A_n)` is the integral over `A₀ × ⋯ × A_{n-1}` of the predictive probability `(α H(A_n) + #{i < n | xᵢ ∈ A_n}) / (α + n)`.

results.title: Pólya urn predictive law is invariant under reordering
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The predictive law does not depend on the order of the previous draws.

results.title: Exchangeability of the Blackwell–MacQueen urn
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Exchangeability of the Blackwell–MacQueen urn (Blackwell–MacQueen 1973): relabeling the draws by a permutation does not change their joint law.

results.title: Tie partition of a sequence of draws
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The partition of the indices `{0, …, n-1}` into groups of equal entries of `xs`.

results.title: Blocks of the tie partition are classes of equal entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Two indices lie in the same block of `tiePartition xs` iff the entries agree.

results.title: Characterization of the tie partition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `tiePartition xs = π` iff equal entries are exactly the pairs in a common block of `π`.

results.title: Tie partition after forgetting the last draw
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Forgetting the last draw restricts the tie partition to the earlier draws.

results.title: Last draw opens a new block iff it is new
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Where the last draw sits: a new table iff it differs from all earlier draws.

results.title: Last draw joins a block iff it matches that block
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Where the last draw sits: at the table `B` iff it equals the earlier draws in `B`.

results.title: Measurability of the tie partition event
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The event that the draws have a given tie partition is measurable.

results.title: The ties of the Blackwell–MacQueen urn follow the Chinese restaurant process
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The ties of the Blackwell–MacQueen urn follow the Chinese restaurant process (Pitman 2006, §3.1): for an atomless base measure, the partition of the first `n` draws into groups of equal values has the law `α^{|π|} ∏_{B ∈ π} (|B| - 1)! / α^{(n)}`.

results.title: Moments of the Dirichlet process for at most two draws
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `n ≤ 2`, `E[∏_{i<n} G(Aᵢ)] = P(X₀ ∈ A₀, …, X_{n-1} ∈ A_{n-1})` for the Blackwell–MacQueen urn. The case `n ≥ 3` is the wanted `lintegral_dirichletProcess_prod`.

results.title: Admissible exponents for sums and differences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A real number $\theta$ is an admissible exponent when every nonempty finite set $A$ of integers satisfies $|A+A|/|A| \le (|A-A|/|A|)^{\theta}$, where $A+A$ and $A-A$ are the sumset and the difference set of $A$.

results.title: The single-set sum-difference exponent
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The single-set sum-difference exponent $C_{3d}$ is the infimum of the admissible exponents, that is, of the set of real numbers $\theta$ such that $|A+A|/|A| \le (|A-A|/|A|)^{\theta}$ for every nonempty finite set $A$ of integers, where $A+A$ and $A-A$ are the sumset and the difference set of $A$.

results.title: The proposition that the single-set sum-difference exponent equals 2
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the statement that the single-set sum-difference exponent $C_{3d}$ is equal to $2$.

results.title: The single-set sum-difference exponent equals 2
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The single-set sum-difference exponent $C_{3d}$ is equal to $2$.

results.title: Wire count of a flat circuit
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The wire count of a flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs, given as a list of gates, is the sum over its gates of the lengths of their predecessor lists: every reference of a gate to a gate index is counted, with multiplicity, while input variables and constants contribute nothing and the modulus of a mod gate is not counted.

results.title: Longest common subsequence by dynamic programming
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given lists $x = x_1 \cdots x_m$ and $y = y_1 \cdots y_n$ over a type with a boolean equality test, fill a table $c_{i,j}$ for $0 \le i \le m$ and $0 \le j \le n$ by $c_{i,0} = c_{0,j} = 0$, by $c_{i,j} = c_{i-1,j-1} + 1$ when the test reports $x_i = y_j$, and by $c_{i,j} = \max(c_{i-1,j}, c_{i,j-1})$ otherwise. Then build a witness $w$ by walking back from $(m, n)$ until $i = 0$ or $j = 0$: when the test reports…

results.title: Correctness of the longest common subsequence algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type whose boolean equality test agrees with equality, let $x$ and $y$ be lists over $\alpha$, and let $(k, w)$ be the pair returned by the dynamic-programming longest common subsequence algorithm on $x$ and $y$. Then $w$ has length $k$, $w$ is a subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) of both $x$ and $y$, and every common subsequence of $x$ and $y$ has length at most the length of $w$.

results.title: Running time of the longest common subsequence algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For lists $x$ and $y$ of lengths $m$ and $n$ over a type with a boolean equality test, the abstract time of the dynamic-programming longest common subsequence algorithm on $x$ and $y$ (its number of table and reconstruction transitions) is at most $mn + (m + n)$.

results.title: Game tree
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A game tree with values in a type $\alpha$ is either a leaf, which carries a value in $\alpha$ (the value of a terminal position), or an inner node, which carries a finite list of game trees (the positions reachable in one move; the list may be empty). Game trees are built inductively, so every game tree is finite.

results.title: Number of leaves
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The number of leaves of a game tree is defined recursively: a leaf counts $1$, and an inner node counts the total number of leaves of its children (so an inner node without children counts $0$).

results.title: Number of leaves of a list of game trees
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The number of leaves of a finite list of game trees is the sum of the numbers of leaves of its members ($0$ for the empty list).

results.title: Alpha-beta pruning
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a player $p$ to move and values $a$ and $b$ in a linear order, alpha-beta pruning with window $[a, b]$ returns the value of a leaf at a cost of one unit (one leaf evaluation), and on an inner node runs the alpha-beta scan of its children for $p$ with window $[a, b]$.

results.title: Alpha-beta scan of the children
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given the player $p$ to move, values $a$ and $b$ in a linear order and a list of game trees (the children of a position), the scan runs alpha-beta pruning for the other player on the children in order, each time with the current bounds $a$ and $b$. The maximizer replaces $a$ by $\max(a, v)$, where $v$ is the child's returned value, and stops as soon as $b \le a$, returning the new $a$; if it never stops early it…

results.title: Lower bound for the maximizer's scan
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let values lie in a linear order. For all values $a$ and $b$ and every finite list of game trees, the value returned by the alpha-beta scan of the list with the maximizer to move and window $[a, b]$ is at least $a$.

results.title: The minimizer's alpha-beta scan stays at or below its upper bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all values $a, b$ in a linear order and every list $ts$ of game trees, the value returned by the alpha-beta scan of $ts$ for the minimizer with lower bound $a$ and upper bound $b$ is at most $b$.

results.title: Alpha-beta never evaluates more leaves than the tree has
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For either player $p$ to move and all values $a, b$ in a linear order, alpha-beta pruning run on a game tree $t$ for $p$ with window $[a, b]$ evaluates at most as many leaves as $t$ has, each leaf evaluation costing one unit.

results.title: Cost of the alpha-beta scan
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For either player $p$, all values $a, b$ in a linear order and every list $ts$ of game trees, the alpha-beta scan of $ts$ for $p$ with lower bound $a$ and upper bound $b$ evaluates at most as many leaves as the trees in $ts$ have in total, each leaf evaluation costing one unit.

results.title: Minimax value
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let values lie in a bounded linear order. The minimax value of a game tree with player $p$ to move (the maximizer or the minimizer) is defined recursively: a leaf is worth the value it carries; an inner node is worth, for the maximizer, the maximum of the minimax values of its children with the minimizer to move, and for the minimizer, the minimum of the minimax values of its children with the maximizer to move. An…

results.title: Minimax value of a list of positions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let values lie in a bounded linear order. For a player $p$ and a finite list of game trees, the value for $p$ is the best of their minimax values with the other player to move: for the maximizer, the maximum of these values, or $\bot$ if the list is empty; for the minimizer, the minimum of these values, or $\top$ if the list is empty.

results.title: Alpha-beta is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Alpha-beta is correct (Knuth and Moore 1975, Theorem 1): for `a ≤ b`, the result of alpha-beta agrees with the minimax value after clamping both to the window `[a, b]`.

results.title: Correctness of the alpha-beta scan
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be the player to move, $ts$ a list of game trees with values in a bounded linear order, and $a \le b$. Let $r$ be the value returned by the alpha-beta scan of $ts$ for $p$ with window $[a, b]$, and let $m$ be the best value for $p$ among $ts$: the maximum of the minimax values of the trees in $ts$ for the minimizer ($\bot$ if $ts$ is empty) when $p$ is the maximizer, and the minimum of their minimax values…

results.title: Alpha-beta fails low when the minimax value is at most the lower bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a game tree with values in a bounded linear order, $p$ the player to move and $a < b$ values. If the minimax value of $t$ for $p$ is at most $a$, then alpha-beta pruning run on $t$ for $p$ with the window $[a, b]$ returns a value at most $a$.

results.title: Alpha-beta is exact inside the window
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a game tree with values in a bounded linear order, $p$ the player to move and $a, b$ values. If the minimax value $v$ of $t$ for $p$ satisfies $a < v < b$, then alpha-beta pruning run on $t$ for $p$ with the window $[a, b]$ returns exactly $v$.

results.title: Alpha-beta at or above the top of the window
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let values lie in a bounded linear order, let $t$ be a game tree, let $p$ be a player, and let $a < b$. If the minimax value of $t$ with $p$ to move is at least $b$, then the value returned by alpha-beta pruning on $t$ with $p$ to move and window $[a, b]$ is at least $b$.

results.title: Alpha-beta with the full window returns the minimax value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a game tree whose values lie in a bounded linear order with least element $\bot$ and greatest element $\top$. For either player $p$ to move, alpha-beta pruning run on $t$ for $p$ with the window $[\bot, \top]$ returns exactly the minimax value of $t$ for $p$.
